claim: SARM1 plays a central, pro-degenerative role in programmed axon death (including Wallerian degeneration).
source: Sterile alpha and TIR motif-containing protein 1 (SARM1) plays a central, pro-degenerative role in programmed axon death (including Wallerian degeneration) (Osterloh et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Osterloh et al., 2012

claim: The axon degeneration pathway is activated in a number of neurodegenerative contexts, including in human disease.
source: This axon degeneration pathway is activated in a number of neurodegenerative contexts, including in human disease (Coleman and Höke, 2020; Gilley et al., 2021; Huppke et al., 2019; Lukacs et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coleman and Höke, 2020; Gilley et al., 2021; Huppke et al., 2019; Lukacs et al., 2019

claim: SARM1 has a critical nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) cleavage (NADase) activity.
source: SARM1 has a critical nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) cleavage (NADase) activity, which is activated when its upstream regulator and axon survival factor nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase 2 (NMNAT2) is depleted or inactive (Essuman et al., 2017; Gilley et al., 2015; Gilley and Coleman, 2010; Sasaki et al., 2020a, Sasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Essuman et al., 2017; Gilley et al., 2015; Gilley and Coleman, 2010; Sasaki et al., 2020a, Sasaki et al., 2016

claim: SARM1 NADase activity is activated when NMNAT2 is depleted or inactive.
source: SARM1 has a critical nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) cleavage (NADase) activity, which is activated when its upstream regulator and axon survival factor nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase 2 (NMNAT2) is depleted or inactive (Essuman et al., 2017; Gilley et al., 2015; Gilley and Coleman, 2010; Sasaki et al., 2020a, Sasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Essuman et al., 2017; Gilley et al., 2015; Gilley and Coleman, 2010; Sasaki et al., 2020a, Sasaki et al., 2016

claim: NMNAT2 loss causes accumulation of its substrate nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
source: NMNAT2 loss causes accumulation of its substrate nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which promotes axon degeneration (Di Stefano et al., 2017; Loreto et al., 2020; Loreto et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Stefano et al., 2017; Loreto et al., 2020; Loreto et al., 2015

claim: NMN accumulation promotes axon degeneration.
source: NMNAT2 loss causes accumulation of its substrate nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which promotes axon degeneration (Di Stefano et al., 2017; Loreto et al., 2020; Loreto et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Stefano et al., 2017; Loreto et al., 2020; Loreto et al., 2015

claim: NMN activates SARM1 NADase activity.
source: NMN is now known to activate SARM1 NADase activity (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019

claim: Sarm1 deletion confers robust axon protection.
source: Given that Sarm1 deletion confers robust axon protection, and even lifelong protection against lethality caused by NMNAT2 deficiency (Gilley et al., 2017), SARM1 has become a very attractive therapeutic target to prevent neurodegeneration.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilley et al., 2017

claim: Sarm1 deletion confers lifelong protection against lethality caused by NMNAT2 deficiency.
source: Given that Sarm1 deletion confers robust axon protection, and even lifelong protection against lethality caused by NMNAT2 deficiency (Gilley et al., 2017), SARM1 has become a very attractive therapeutic target to prevent neurodegeneration.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilley et al., 2017

claim: SARM1 has become a very attractive therapeutic target to prevent neurodegeneration.
source: Given that Sarm1 deletion confers robust axon protection, and even lifelong protection against lethality caused by NMNAT2 deficiency (Gilley et al., 2017), SARM1 has become a very attractive therapeutic target to prevent neurodegeneration.
evidence: Inference based on the protective effects of Sarm1 deletion and citation to Gilley et al., 2017

claim: An allosteric pocket exists in SARM1 armadillo-repeat (ARM) domain which is important for the regulation of SARM1 activity.
source: Recent structural data revealed the existence of an allosteric pocket in SARM1 armadillo-repeat (ARM) domain which is important for the regulation of SARM1 activity.
evidence: Supported by reference to recent structural data

claim: NMN binds to the allosteric pocket in SARM1 ARM domain, leading to SARM1 activation.
source: NMN binds to this pocket, leading to SARM1 activation (Figley et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Figley et al., 2021

claim: NAD can bind the same allosteric site as NMN in SARM1 ARM domain, competing with NMN to prevent SARM1 activation.
source: NAD (Jiang et al., 2020) can also bind the same allosteric site, competing with NMN to prevent SARM1 activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2020

claim: The ratio between NMN:NAD is important to regulate SARM1 activity.
source: The ratio between NMN:NAD is therefore important to regulate SARM1 activity (Figley et al., 2021) and we have recently extended this to show that, at physiological levels, changes in NMN levels have the greater impact on the regulation of SARM1 activity (Angeletti et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Figley et al., 2021 and Angeletti et al., 2021

claim: At physiological levels, changes in NMN levels have the greater impact on the regulation of SARM1 activity compared to NAD.
source: The ratio between NMN:NAD is therefore important to regulate SARM1 activity (Figley et al., 2021) and we have recently extended this to show that, at physiological levels, changes in NMN levels have the greater impact on the regulation of SARM1 activity (Angeletti et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Angeletti et al., 2021

claim: Vacor is a disused pesticide and powerful neurotoxin associated with human peripheral and central nervous system disorders.
source: Here, we have investigated whether vacor, a disused pesticide and powerful neurotoxin associated with human peripheral and central nervous system disorders (Gallanosa et al., 1981; LeWitt, 1980) and axon degeneration in rats (Watson and Griffin, 1987), causes activation of programmed axon death.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gallanosa et al., 1981; LeWitt, 1980

claim: Vacor is associated with axon degeneration in rats.
source: Here, we have investigated whether vacor, a disused pesticide and powerful neurotoxin associated with human peripheral and central nervous system disorders (Gallanosa et al., 1981; LeWitt, 1980) and axon degeneration in rats (Watson and Griffin, 1987), causes activation of programmed axon death.
evidence: Supported by citation to Watson and Griffin, 1987

claim: Vacor is a pyridine derivative that is metabolised to vacor mononucleotide (VMN) and vacor adenine dinucleotide (VAD) through a two-step conversion by NAMPT and NMNAT2.
source: Vacor is a pyridine derivative that is metabolised to vacor mononucleotide (VMN) and vacor adenine dinucleotide (VAD) through a two-step conversion by nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) and NMNAT2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: VAD inhibits NMNAT2.
source: Considering VAD inhibits SARM1 regulator NMNAT2 (Buonvicino et al., 2018), we reasoned that vacor may induce SARM1-dependent axon death.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buonvicino et al., 2018

claim: Vacor neurotoxicity is entirely mediated by SARM1.
source: We demonstrate that vacor neurotoxicity is entirely mediated by SARM1 such that Sarm1-/- neurons and their axons are completely resistant.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data showing Sarm1-/- neurons are completely resistant to vacor

claim: Sarm1-/- neurons and their axons are completely resistant to vacor.
source: We demonstrate that vacor neurotoxicity is entirely mediated by SARM1 such that Sarm1-/- neurons and their axons are completely resistant.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript

claim: Vacor metabolite VMN directly binds to and activates SARM1, causing neuronal death.
source: We unexpectedly find that vacor metabolite VMN directly binds to and activates SARM1, causing neuronal death.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data including ITC binding studies and NADase activity assays

claim: VMN and VAD are generated in vacor-treated dorsal root ganglion (DRG) mouse neurons.
source: We first confirmed that VMN and VAD are generated in vacor-treated dorsal root ganglion (DRG) mouse neurons (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: Confirmed by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: DRG and SCG mouse neurons exhibit rapid, dose-dependent neurite degeneration in response to vacor treatment.
source: and that these and a second neuron type, superior cervical ganglia (SCG) mouse neurons, exhibit rapid, dose-dependent neurite degeneration (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by phase contrast imaging and quantification shown in Figure 1C-F

claim: Nicotinamide (NAM) delays vacor-induced neurite degeneration.
source: Consistent with the proposed toxic role for vacor metabolites (Buonvicino et al., 2018), both nicotinamide (NAM), which competes with vacor as a preferred substrate for NAMPT, and the NAMPT inhibitor FK866 (Figure 1A), delayed vacor-induced neurite degeneration (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H

claim: FK866 delays vacor-induced neurite degeneration.
source: Consistent with the proposed toxic role for vacor metabolites (Buonvicino et al., 2018), both nicotinamide (NAM), which competes with vacor as a preferred substrate for NAMPT, and the NAMPT inhibitor FK866 (Figure 1A), delayed vacor-induced neurite degeneration (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1I-J

claim: NAM competes with vacor as a preferred substrate for NAMPT.
source: Consistent with the proposed toxic role for vacor metabolites (Buonvicino et al., 2018), both nicotinamide (NAM), which competes with vacor as a preferred substrate for NAMPT, and the NAMPT inhibitor FK866 (Figure 1A), delayed vacor-induced neurite degeneration (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: Stated as known mechanism and consistent with cited literature

claim: NAM was an effective treatment for patients with vacor poisoning.
source: Such competition may explain why NAM was an effective treatment for patients with vacor poisoning (Gallanosa et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallanosa et al., 1981

claim: Vacor failed to induce degeneration of Sarm1-/- DRG and SCG neurites.
source: As hypothesised, vacor failed to induce degeneration of Sarm1-/- DRG and SCG neurites (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D

claim: Sarm1-/- neurites survive indefinitely even after multiple vacor doses.
source: This protection was extremely strong, with neurites surviving indefinitely even after multiple vacor doses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Sarm1-/- neurites continue to grow normally even with repeated vacor dosing.
source: Sarm1-/- neurites were not only protected from degeneration, but they also continued to grow normally, even with repeated dosing (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by neurite outgrowth measurements shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: Nmnat2 null axons are permanently rescued and continue to grow in the absence of SARM1.
source: This mirrors the permanent rescue and continued growth previously reported in Nmnat2 null axons in the absence of SARM1 (Gilley et al., 2017; Gilley et al., 2015), suggesting complete efficacy in both toxic and inherited types of neuropathy.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gilley et al., 2017; Gilley et al., 2015

claim: Vacor neurotoxicity is predominantly SARM1-dependent.
source: This mirrors the permanent rescue and continued growth previously reported in Nmnat2 null axons in the absence of SARM1 (Gilley et al., 2017; Gilley et al., 2015), suggesting complete efficacy in both toxic and inherited types of neuropathy. It also shows that vacor neurotoxicity is predominantly SARM1-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the complete protection of Sarm1-/- neurons from vacor toxicity

claim: Exogenous expression of wild-type human SARM1 in Sarm1-/- SCG neurons restores vacor sensitivity.
source: Exogenous expression of wild-type human SARM1 (hSARM1) in Sarm1-/- SCG neurons restored vacor sensitivity, whereas expression of E642A hSARM1, which lacks NADase activity, did not (Figure 2G–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H), similar to findings in axotomy (Essuman et al., 2017).
evidence: Demonstrated by microinjection experiments shown in Figure 2G-I

claim: Expression of E642A hSARM1, which lacks NADase activity, does not restore vacor sensitivity in Sarm1-/- SCG neurons.
source: Exogenous expression of wild-type human SARM1 (hSARM1) in Sarm1-/- SCG neurons restored vacor sensitivity, whereas expression of E642A hSARM1, which lacks NADase activity, did not (Figure 2G–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H), similar to findings in axotomy (Essuman et al., 2017).
evidence: Demonstrated by microinjection experiments shown in Figure 2G-I

claim: SARM1 NADase activity is the critical function required for vacor toxicity.
source: We therefore tested if SARM1 NADase activity is the critical function required for vacor toxicity. Exogenous expression of wild-type human SARM1 (hSARM1) in Sarm1-/- SCG neurons restored vacor sensitivity, whereas expression of E642A hSARM1, which lacks NADase activity, did not (Figure 2G–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H), similar to findings in axotomy (Essuman et al., 2017).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing wild-type and E642A mutant SARM1 in rescue experiments

claim: Activation of the pathway by vacor causes SARM1-dependent cell death.
source: Interestingly, unlike axotomy, activation of the pathway by vacor also caused SARM1-dependent cell death (Figure 2I), similar to that previously reported with constitutively active SARM1 (Gerdts et al., 2015; Gerdts et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by viable neuron counts in Figure 2I and supported by citations to Gerdts et al., 2015; Gerdts et al., 2013

claim: Addition of vacor to either the neurite or soma compartment directly activates local death of cell bodies and/or neurites.
source: Addition of vacor to either compartment directly activated local death of cell bodies and/or neurites.
evidence: Demonstrated by microfluidic chamber experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Vacor-induced cell death causes neurite degeneration, but vacor-induced neurite degeneration does not cause cell loss.
source: However, while vacor-induced cell death also causes neurite degeneration, the reverse was not true: no cell loss was observed after local induction of distal neurite degeneration by vacor (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by microfluidic chamber experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: Vacor causes a global loss of photoreceptor neuronal activity in the retina.
source: Electroretinogram (ERG) recordings showed that vacor caused a global loss of photoreceptor neuronal activity, and subsequent loss of bipolar and retinal ganglion cell (RGC) responses, which were fully rescued by SARM1 deficiency (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG recordings shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Vacor causes loss of bipolar and retinal ganglion cell (RGC) responses.
source: Electroretinogram (ERG) recordings showed that vacor caused a global loss of photoreceptor neuronal activity, and subsequent loss of bipolar and retinal ganglion cell (RGC) responses, which were fully rescued by SARM1 deficiency (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG recordings shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: SARM1 deficiency fully rescues vacor-induced loss of photoreceptor, bipolar, and RGC responses.
source: Electroretinogram (ERG) recordings showed that vacor caused a global loss of photoreceptor neuronal activity, and subsequent loss of bipolar and retinal ganglion cell (RGC) responses, which were fully rescued by SARM1 deficiency (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG recordings comparing wild-type and Sarm1-/- mice shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Vacor administration causes inner retina neuronal death, as revealed by a significant reduction in RGC number.
source: Vacor administration also caused inner retina neuronal death, as revealed by a significant reduction in RGC number. Again, this was completely prevented by SARM1 deficiency (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by RGC counts shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: SARM1 deficiency completely prevents vacor-induced reduction in RGC number.
source: Vacor administration also caused inner retina neuronal death, as revealed by a significant reduction in RGC number. Again, this was completely prevented by SARM1 deficiency (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by RGC counts comparing wild-type and Sarm1-/- mice shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: The absence of SARM1 confers functional and morphological protection of neurons against vacor toxicity in vivo.
source: These data demonstrate that the absence of SARM1 confers functional and morphological protection of neurons against vacor toxicity in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG recordings and RGC counts in vivo

claim: SARM1 activation depletes NAD in neurons.
source: Activation of SARM1 depletes NAD and generates cADPR in neurons (Essuman et al., 2017; Gerdts et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2020a, Sasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Essuman et al., 2017; Gerdts et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2020a, Sasaki et al., 2016

claim: SARM1 activation generates cADPR in neurons.
source: Activation of SARM1 depletes NAD and generates cADPR in neurons (Essuman et al., 2017; Gerdts et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2020a, Sasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Essuman et al., 2017; Gerdts et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2020a, Sasaki et al., 2016

claim: SARM1 activation was confirmed by a drastic SARM1-dependent decline in NAD following vacor administration.
source: Surprisingly, while SARM1 activation was confirmed by a drastic SARM1-dependent decline in NAD and increase in cADPR following vacor administration, NMN did not rise and even fell slightly (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 4A-D

claim: SARM1 activation was confirmed by an increase in cADPR following vacor administration.
source: Surprisingly, while SARM1 activation was confirmed by a drastic SARM1-dependent decline in NAD and increase in cADPR following vacor administration, NMN did not rise and even fell slightly (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 4A-D

claim: NMN did not rise and even fell slightly following vacor administration.
source: Surprisingly, while SARM1 activation was confirmed by a drastic SARM1-dependent decline in NAD and increase in cADPR following vacor administration, NMN did not rise and even fell slightly (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 4A-D

claim: NMN and NAD levels and their ratio to one another were not altered in vacor-treated Sarm1-/- neurons.
source: Furthermore, NMN and NAD levels and their ratio to one another were not altered in our vacor-treated Sarm1-/- neurons (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that the reported inhibition of NAMPT and NMNAT2 by vacor/VAD (Buonvicino et al., 2018) does not occur in this context at this drug concentration.
evidence: Demonstrated by metabolite measurements in Sarm1-/- neurons shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: The reported inhibition of NAMPT and NMNAT2 by vacor/VAD does not occur in this context at this drug concentration.
source: Furthermore, NMN and NAD levels and their ratio to one another were not altered in our vacor-treated Sarm1-/- neurons (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that the reported inhibition of NAMPT and NMNAT2 by vacor/VAD (Buonvicino et al., 2018) does not occur in this context at this drug concentration.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of change in NMN and NAD levels in Sarm1-/- neurons

claim: NMN deamidase strongly preserves axotomised axons by preventing NMN accumulation.
source: Crucially, NMN deamidase, an enzyme that strongly preserves axotomised axons by preventing NMN accumulation (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Di Stefano et al., 2017; Di Stefano et al., 2015; Loreto et al., 2015), was also unable to protect against vacor toxicity (Figure 4E and F)
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Stefano et al., 2017; Di Stefano et al., 2015; Loreto et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 4E

claim: NMN deamidase was unable to protect against vacor toxicity.
source: Crucially, NMN deamidase, an enzyme that strongly preserves axotomised axons by preventing NMN accumulation (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Di Stefano et al., 2017; Di Stefano et al., 2015; Loreto et al., 2015), was also unable to protect against vacor toxicity (Figure 4E and F)
evidence: Demonstrated by microinjection experiments shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: Recombinant NMN deamidase retains its ability to convert NMN to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) in the presence of vacor, VMN and VAD.
source: even though recombinant NMN deamidase retains its ability to convert NMN to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) in the presence of vacor, VMN and VAD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: WLDS failed to rescue neurons against vacor neurotoxicity.
source: WLDS, another enzyme that limits NMN accumulation (Di Stefano et al., 2015), also failed to rescue neurons against vacor neurotoxicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: In this specific context, NMN is not responsible for SARM1 activation by vacor.
source: These data suggest that, in this specific context at least, NMN is not responsible for SARM1 activation.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of NMN accumulation and failure of NMN deamidase to protect

claim: VMN potently activates the NADase activity of recombinant hSARM1.
source: Crucially, we found that VMN potently activates the NADase activity of recombinant hSARM1, even more so than NMN, having a lower Ka and resulting in a greater induction (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by NADase activity assays shown in Figure 5A

claim: VMN activates hSARM1 NADase activity more potently than NMN, having a lower Ka and resulting in a greater induction.
source: Crucially, we found that VMN potently activates the NADase activity of recombinant hSARM1, even more so than NMN, having a lower Ka and resulting in a greater induction (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by NADase activity assays and kinetic analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: VAD only had a weak inhibitory effect on hSARM1 activity.
source: Conversely, VAD only had a weak inhibitory effect on hSARM1 activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by NADase activity assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Recombinant hSARM1 NADase activity dropped at higher VMN concentrations.
source: Intriguingly, recombinant hSARM1 NADase activity dropped at higher VMN concentrations (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by NADase activity assays shown in Figure 5A

claim: The data are compatible with two distinct binding sites of VMN on SARM1.
source: Analysis via best fitting (see equation in Materials and methods) suggests that our data are compatible with two distinct binding sites of VMN on SARM1 and led us to establish binding constants for activation (Ka) and inhibition (Ki) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Inferred from kinetic analysis of NADase activity data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Exogenous application of VMN induces SARM1-dependent death of uninjured DRG neurites.
source: However, we now show that exogenous application of its analogue, VMN, does induce SARM1-dependent death of uninjured DRG neurites (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by neurite degeneration assays shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: Exogenous NMN does not induce degeneration of uninjured neurites when NMNAT2 is present.
source: While NMN activates SARM1 (Zhao et al., 2019) and promotes programmed axon death when NMNAT2 is depleted (Di Stefano et al., 2017; Loreto et al., 2020; Loreto et al., 2015), exogenous NMN does not induce degeneration of uninjured neurites (Di Stefano et al., 2015), probably because it is rapidly converted to NAD when NMNAT2 is present.
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Stefano et al., 2015 and explained by known metabolism

claim: VMN is a more potent activator of SARM1 than NMN.
source: This difference likely reflects a combination of VMN being both a more potent activator of SARM1 and it accumulating more because it is not efficiently metabolised by NMNAT2 (Buonvicino et al., 2018).
evidence: Demonstrated by NADase activity assays and supported by citation to Buonvicino et al., 2018

claim: VMN accumulates more than NMN because it is not efficiently metabolised by NMNAT2.
source: This difference likely reflects a combination of VMN being both a more potent activator of SARM1 and it accumulating more because it is not efficiently metabolised by NMNAT2 (Buonvicino et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buonvicino et al., 2018

claim: VMN is not a substrate of NMN deamidase.
source: First, unlike NMN, VMN is not a substrate of NMN deamidase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), thus explaining its inability to protect against vacor neurotoxicity (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: VMN is not a substrate of the nuclear isoform NMNAT1.
source: In addition, VMN is not a substrate of the nuclear isoform NMNAT1 and is a poor substrate of mitochondrial NMNAT3 (Buonvicino et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Buonvicino et al., 2018

claim: VMN is a poor substrate of mitochondrial NMNAT3.
source: In addition, VMN is not a substrate of the nuclear isoform NMNAT1 and is a poor substrate of mitochondrial NMNAT3 (Buonvicino et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Buonvicino et al., 2018

claim: VMN accumulation in cell bodies and subsequent SARM1 activation provides a rationale for why vacor administration causes cell death.
source: so VMN accumulation in cell bodies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and subsequent SARM1 activation, as detected by a rise of cADPR in this compartment (Figure 4D), provides a clear rationale for why vacor administration also causes cell death.
evidence: Inferred from VMN accumulation data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and cADPR measurements (Figure 4D)

claim: SARM1 ARM domain is believed to maintain SARM1 in an inhibited state.
source: SARM1 ARM domain is believed to maintain SARM1 in an inhibited state (Figley et al., 2021; Gerdts et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Figley et al., 2021; Gerdts et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2020

claim: SARM1 is activated by NMN binding directly to the ARM domain.
source: SARM1 is activated by NMN binding directly to the ARM domain (Figley et al., 2021; Gu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Figley et al., 2021; Gu et al., 2021

claim: VMN bound to dSARM1ARM with a Kd value of 2.83 ± 0.16 μM (1:1 molar ratio).
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) analysis showed that VMN bound to dSARM1ARM with a Kd value of 2.83 ± 0.16 μM (1:1 molar ratio) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ITC analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: The crystal structure of VMN-bound dSARM1ARM was determined at 1.69 Å resolution.
source: To further characterise this interaction, we determined the crystal structure of the VMN-bound dSARM1ARM (1.69 Å resolution).
evidence: Stated as experimental result

claim: dSARM1ARM contains eight tandem armadillo repeats (ARM1-8) stacking into an unusually compact right-handed superhelix.
source: dSARM1ARM contains eight tandem armadillo repeats (ARM1-8) stacking into an unusually compact right-handed superhelix (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by crystal structure shown in Figure 6A

claim: The bound VMN molecule sits in the central groove of dSARM1ARM, which is mainly lined by the H3 helices from ARM1-5.
source: The bound VMN molecule sits in the central groove of dSARM1ARM, which is mainly lined by the H3 helices from ARM1-5 (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by crystal structure shown in Figure 6A

claim: The interaction between VMN and dSARM1ARM is mediated by two pi-stacking interactions and eight hydrogen bonds.
source: The interaction is mediated by two pi-stacking interactions between the indole of W385 and the pyridine moiety of VMN, and between the imidazole ring of H392 and the nitrobenzene moiety of VMN (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B); and eight hydrogen bonds, with a buried surface area of ~910 Å2 (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: VMN has over two-fold higher affinity for dSARM1ARM than NMN (Kd = 6.39 ± 0.04 μM).
source: Our data show that VMN has over two-fold higher affinity for dSARM1ARM than NMN (Kd = 6.39 ± 0.04 μM), whose own interaction with the ARM domain was recently reported (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Figley et al., 2021).
evidence: Demonstrated by ITC analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation to Figley et al., 2021

claim: VMN-bound dSARM1ARM adopts a similar conformation to NMN-bound dSARM1ARM.
source: VMN-bound dSARM1ARM adopts a similar conformation to NMN-bound dSARM1ARM (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 6C

claim: The NMN moiety of VMN and NMN share the same binding mode in dSARM1ARM.
source: Comparison of the two structures reveals that the NMN moiety of VMN and NMN share the same binding mode, with the key residues involved in NMN binding interacting with the analogous portions of the VMN molecule (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 6B

claim: VMN forms different and extra interactions compared to NMN in the dSARM1ARM binding pocket.
source: Importantly, in the NMN-bound structure, NMN forms a hydrogen bond with the residues H599 and G600 (loop connecting ARM6 and 7), while in the VMN-bound structure, due to the extra portion of VMN (urea and nitrobenzene groups) extending to the region between the N- and C-termini of the protein, two different hydrogen bonds are formed between VMN and H392 (ARM2 H1) at the N-terminus, and N640 (ARM8 H1) at the C-terminus. Furthermore, the pi-stacking interaction between H392 and the nitrobenzene of VMN is specific to this compound.
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison

claim: The different and extra interactions VMN forms could explain why VMN induces SARM1 activation more efficiently compared to NMN.
source: These different and extra interactions VMN forms could explain why VMN induces SARM1 activation more efficiently, compared to NMN.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis

claim: The compaction seen in both NMN and VMN-bound dSARM1ARM structures likely represents the conformation of the ARM domain in active SARM1.
source: The compaction seen in both NMN and VMN-bound dSARM1ARM structures likely represents the conformation of the ARM domain in active SARM1, based on the comparison with the more open crystal structures of ligand-free and NaMN-bound dSARM1ARM, as well as cryo-EM (electron microscopy) structures of ligand-free and NAD-bound hSARM1, representing the inactive state of the protein (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021; Sporny et al., 2020) (Figure 6C).
evidence: Inferred from structural comparisons shown in Figure 6C and supported by citations to Bratkowski et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021; Sporny et al., 2020

claim: NaMN stabilises the open conformation of dSARM1ARM and is unable to form interactions with the C-terminal region of the protein.
source: NaMN stabilises the open conformation of dSARM1ARM due to the rotation of its nicotinic acid (NA) portion towards the N-terminus of the protein, and is therefore unable to form any interactions with the C-terminal region of the protein (Sasaki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2021

claim: The adenine group and adjacent ribose of NAD would cause steric clashes with the C-terminal region of the protein in the VMN-bound structure conformation.
source: In the NAD-bound hSARM1ARM structure, the portion of NAD equivalent to NMN and VMN interacts with the protein through similar interactions, but the adenine group and the adjacent ribose of NAD extend further down to the side of the region between the termini. This would cause steric clashes with the C-terminal region of the protein, particularly with the loop connecting ARM6 and 7 (residues 594–602), thus preventing NAD from inducing a more compact conformation in the ARM domain (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), keeping the protein in the inactive state.
evidence: Demonstrated by structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: VMN activates SARM1 with a mechanism similar to NMN, inducing a compaction of the ARM domain.
source: In summary, our data suggest that VMN activates SARM1 with a mechanism similar to NMN, but with some important differences, inducing a compaction of the ARM domain, destabilising its interfaces with the neighbouring ARM, SAM, and TIR domains, and eventually permitting the TIR domains to self-associate and hydrolyse NAD.
evidence: Inferred from structural data and mechanistic understanding

claim: W103A, R157A, and K193R mutations in human SARM1 prevent restoration of vacor sensitivity in Sarm1-/- SCG neurons.
source: We introduced the corresponding W103A, R157A, and K193R mutations into human SARM1 and exogenously expressed them in Sarm1-/- SCG mouse neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). Unlike wild-type hSARM1, these mutants failed to restore neurite degeneration and cell death after vacor administration (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by microinjection experiments shown in Figure 7A-F

claim: Neither VMN nor NMN could activate the NADase activity of recombinant K193R hSARM1.
source: Crucially, neither VMN nor NMN could activate the NADase activity of recombinant K193R hSARM1 (Figure 7G).
evidence: Demonstrated by NADase activity assays shown in Figure 7G

claim: VMN is the most potent activator of SARM1 reported so far.
source: To our knowledge, VMN is the most potent activator of SARM1 reported so far, and our structural data reveal essential information on SARM1 regulation which will aid drug development to block SARM1 activation.
evidence: Based on comparison of VMN activation potency with NMN and other known activators

claim: Vacor use is banned.
source: Vacor use is banned, but structurally related pyridines are widely-used and present in drugs, pesticides and food, raising important questions about their potential toxicity and SARM1 as a mediator of environmental neurotoxicity.
evidence: Stated as fact

claim: Structurally related pyridines to vacor are widely-used and present in drugs, pesticides and food.
source: Vacor use is banned, but structurally related pyridines are widely-used and present in drugs, pesticides and food, raising important questions about their potential toxicity and SARM1 as a mediator of environmental neurotoxicity.
evidence: Stated as fact and supported by citation to Adams and De Kimpe, 2006; Li et al., 2016

claim: 3-acetyl pyridine is associated with axon degeneration.
source: Indeed, one other nicotinamide analog, 3-acetyl pyridine, is already associated with axon degeneration (Desclin and Escubi, 1974) and subsequent to our preprint of this work has now been reported to act through SARM1 in a similar manner (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Desclin and Escubi, 1974 and Wu et al., 2021

claim: 3-acetyl pyridine acts through SARM1 in a similar manner to vacor.
source: Indeed, one other nicotinamide analog, 3-acetyl pyridine, is already associated with axon degeneration (Desclin and Escubi, 1974) and subsequent to our preprint of this work has now been reported to act through SARM1 in a similar manner (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021

claim: Genetic hyperactivation of SARM1 has been associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Genetic hyperactivation of SARM1 has also now been associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Bloom et al., 2021; Gilley et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bloom et al., 2021; Gilley et al., 2021

claim: SARM1 deficiency completely rescues neurons from vacor toxicity and preserves their functionality.
source: Despite the extreme toxicity of vacor, SARM1 deficiency completely rescues neurons and preserves their functionality.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro and in vivo experiments throughout the manuscript

claim: Blocking SARM1 can completely prevent programmed axon death.
source: Together with the previously reported lifelong protection in a genetic model of a rare human axonopathy (Gilley et al., 2017; Lukacs et al., 2019), this further supports the therapeutic potential of blocking SARM1 to completely prevent programmed axon death.
evidence: Inferred from current data and supported by citations to Gilley et al., 2017; Lukacs et al., 2019

claim: Vacor causes pancreatic β-cell destruction and diabetes in humans.
source: Lastly, as vacor causes pancreatic β-cell destruction and diabetes in humans (Gallanosa et al., 1981), these findings could also have broader implications, uncovering a role for SARM1 in the survival of insulin producing cells and aiding research on diabetes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallanosa et al., 1981

claim: Sarm1 deletion does not prevent RGC death following optic nerve crush in mice.
source: Interestingly, it was previously reported that Sarm1 deletion does not prevent RGC death following optic nerve crush in mice (Fernandes et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernandes et al., 2018

claim: SARM1 activation is sufficient to drive degeneration of multiple types of retinal neuron (including RGC) in addition to photoreceptors.
source: However, our data show that SARM1 activation is sufficient to drive degeneration of multiple types of retinal neuron (including RGC) in addition to photoreceptors (Sasaki et al., 2020b), making SARM1 a promising target to treat retinal degeneration, at least in response to certain insults.
evidence: Demonstrated by ERG and RGC count data and supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2020b

claim: Retrograde RGC soma death after axotomy proceeds by a different, SARM1-independent mechanism such as loss of retrogradely delivered trophic factors.
source: To explain these differences, we suggest that retrograde RGC soma death after axotomy proceeds by a different, SARM1-independent mechanism such as loss of retrogradely delivered trophic factors.
evidence: Proposed as speculation to explain differences between studies

claim: Programmed axon death can be aberrantly activated in humans by genetic mutation of NMNAT2.
source: Our data also further implicate programmed axon death in human disease. It appears that this degeneration pathway can be aberrantly activated in humans not only by genetic mutation of NMNAT2 (Huppke et al., 2019; Lukacs et al., 2019), but also by SARM1 activation in severe neurotoxicity within hours of vacor ingestion (LeWitt, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huppke et al., 2019; Lukacs et al., 2019

claim: Programmed axon death can be aberrantly activated in humans by SARM1 activation in severe neurotoxicity within hours of vacor ingestion.
source: Our data also further implicate programmed axon death in human disease. It appears that this degeneration pathway can be aberrantly activated in humans not only by genetic mutation of NMNAT2 (Huppke et al., 2019; Lukacs et al., 2019), but also by SARM1 activation in severe neurotoxicity within hours of vacor ingestion (LeWitt, 1980).
evidence: Inferred from current findings and supported by citation to LeWitt, 1980

claim: Recombinant hSARM1 uses vacor for base exchange to produce VAD.
source: Finally, we have also recently reported that recombinant hSARM1 uses vacor for base exchange to produce VAD (Angeletti et al., 2021), suggesting that vacor can also directly interact with SARM1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Angeletti et al., 2021
